hook.core: Payday. **$254.20** lands in your account. You worked four shifts, including a Saturday. Is that right? Most people just shrug and spend it. But the answer is right there on your payslip, if you know how to read it.

why.support: A payslip uses pay words like **gross** and **net**. Learn them. Then you can check your pay in a minute and catch mistakes.
why.core: A payslip is a short text full of pay words: **gross**, **net**, **rate**, **loading**, **super**. Some of them mean something different from what they mean in everyday life. Once you can read them, you can check every payslip in a minute and catch mistakes before they cost you. Young workers get underpaid more than most. Checking is how you stop it.
why.extend: A payslip is a compact technical text. Its vocabulary (gross, net, loading, penalty, super) often has a different meaning outside work. Reading it closely, checking the details and inferring what's missing lets you catch underpayments early, which matters, because young casual workers are often the ones underpaid.

articles.title: How to read your payslip

body.support:
Every time you're paid, you must get a **payslip** within **one working day**. It uses **pay words**.

**Top:** your boss's business, your name, and the days you're being paid for.

**Hours × rate.** Check your hours. Weekends often pay more. That's a **penalty rate**.

**Gross pay.** Not yuck! It means your **total** pay, before anything comes out.

**Tax.** Some money may go to the tax office. Many students pay little or none.

**Net pay.** What goes into your **bank**.

**Super.** Money saved for when you're older. If you're **under 18**, your boss only pays it in weeks you work **more than 30 hours**.

Something wrong? Check your hours. Then ask your manager, politely. The **Fair Work Ombudsman** can help for free.
body.core:
Every time you're paid, your employer must give you a **payslip** within **one working day**. It might be paper, an email or a page in an app. It's a short text, but it's packed with **pay words**. Some of them mean something different at work from what they mean everywhere else.

**Who and when.** At the top: the employer's name and **ABN**, your name, the **pay period** (the days it covers) and the **pay date**.

**Hours × rate.** Each line shows hours, a **pay rate** and an amount. Check the hours match what you really worked. Weekends, late nights and public holidays often pay more. That's a **penalty rate**. If you're **casual**, your rate usually includes a **casual loading**: extra pay instead of paid holidays and sick days. Under most awards it's 25%.

**Gross pay.** Not gross as in disgusting! **Gross** means your total pay, **before** anything comes out.

**Tax.** Some pay may be taken out as **tax** and sent to the tax office for you. How much depends on what you earn and the form you filled in when you started. Many students working a few shifts have little or none taken.

**Net pay.** What actually lands in your bank: gross pay minus tax.

**Super.** Money your employer pays into a super fund for when you're older. It's usually **12%** on top of your pay. But if you're **under 18**, your employer only has to pay it in weeks you work **more than 30 hours**. So $0 super can be right.

**Year to date (YTD).** Your total since 1 July.

If something looks wrong, check your own record of your hours. Then ask your manager, politely and in writing. Still stuck? The **Fair Work Ombudsman** can help, for free.
body.extend:
By law, your employer must give you a **payslip** within **one working day** of payday. Whether paper, email or app, it's a dense technical text, and several of its terms have different meanings outside the workplace.

**Identifying details.** Employer name and **ABN**, employee name, **pay period** and **pay date**. These are legally required.

**Earnings.** Each line multiplies hours by a **rate**. Verify the hours against your own record. Many awards set **penalty rates** for weekends, nights and public holidays. Casual rates usually include a **casual loading** (25% under most awards), which compensates for not getting paid leave.

**Gross pay.** The total earned before deductions. In this context, *gross* means *whole*, not *disgusting*.

**Tax withheld.** An amount sent to the ATO on your behalf. It depends on your income and on your tax file number declaration. Many students working a few shifts have little or none withheld.

**Net pay.** Gross minus deductions: what reaches your account.

**Super.** The super guarantee is **12%** of ordinary earnings, paid into your fund. For employees **under 18**, though, it's only required in weeks they work **more than 30 hours**. A $0 super line may be correct.

**Year to date (YTD).** Cumulative totals since 1 July.

If something doesn't add up, compare it with your own records, raise it with your manager in writing, and contact the **Fair Work Ombudsman** if it isn't resolved.

caseStudies.title: The bakery that didn't pay up

body.support:
A teenager worked as a casual at a bakery in Brisbane.

A **Fair Work** inspector checked the pay. The inspector believed the worker was paid too little. The **pay rate** was too low. Evening and weekend **penalty rates** were missing.

The inspector told the business to pay the money back. The business didn't.

So Fair Work took them to **court**. Then the worker got paid.

In **2020**, the court fined the business and its manager **$26,460**.

All of these problems show up on a payslip. That's why it pays to check.
body.core:
A teenager had a casual job as a shop assistant at a bakery in Mount Ommaney, in Brisbane.

An inspector from the **Fair Work Ombudsman** looked into the pay. The inspector believed the worker had been paid too little. The problems were with the basic **pay rate**, the **casual loading**, and the **penalty rates** for evenings and weekends.

The inspector gave the business a **compliance notice**. That's an official order. It told the business to work out what it owed the worker and pay it back.

The business didn't do it.

So the Fair Work Ombudsman took it to **court**. Only then was the worker paid what they were owed.

In **December 2020**, the court fined the company **$22,050**, and its manager **$4,410**. That's **$26,460** in total. The judge said they had deliberately ignored their obligations.

Every problem in this case shows up on a payslip: the rate, the loading, and weekend hours paid at the wrong rate. Knowing what to look for is the first step to getting it fixed.
body.extend:
A teenager worked as a casual shop assistant at a bakery in Mount Ommaney, Brisbane.

A **Fair Work Ombudsman** inspector believed the worker had been underpaid under the retail award. Three things were wrong: the minimum wage, the **casual loading**, and the **penalty rates** for evening and weekend work.

The inspector issued a **compliance notice**. This formal direction required the business to calculate what it owed and back-pay it. The business did not comply.

The Fair Work Ombudsman went to court. Only then was the worker back-paid.

In **December 2020**, the Federal Circuit Court fined the company **$22,050** and its manager **$4,410**: **$26,460** in total. The judge found they had deliberately ignored their legal obligations.

Every part of this underpayment (rate, loading, penalty rates) shows up on a payslip. A worker who knows how to read one can spot it. Close reading is the first line of defence.

teacher.overview: Students learn to read a payslip as a technical text: its required parts (employer and ABN, pay period, pay date, hours × rate, gross, tax, net, super, year to date) and its vocabulary, including words with different everyday meanings (gross, net, penalty, loading, super). They check details and calculations, connect what they learn to a real Fair Work Ombudsman case in which a teenage casual was underpaid, and write a polite query about a mistake.
prep: Make or download a sample payslip (the Fair Work Ombudsman has a template) for students who don't have one. Never ask students to bring a payslip in; offer it as an option, with private details covered.
Check the Fair Work Pay Calculator is reachable on school devices.
Optional: ask students with jobs to share (anonymously) what their payslips look like: app, email or paper.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** gross = total before anything is taken out; net = what goes into your bank after tax. Within one working day of payday. Under 18s only get super in weeks they work more than 30 hours.

**Payslip:** 1 employer and ABN; 2 pay period and pay date; 3 hours × rate (Saturday pays more); 4 gross; 5 tax withheld (none here); 6 net; 7 super ($0 is correct); 8 year to date.

**Pay words (samples):** net — a mesh for catching things / pay after tax; rate — speed or score / pay per hour; penalty — a punishment / a higher rate the employer pays for some times; super — great / retirement savings; loading — putting things in / extra pay casuals get instead of paid leave.

**Sort:** 8 × $16.40 — looks right; Saturday at the ordinary rate — check it; payslip late — check it; $0 super — looks right; net $234.20 — check it (should be $254.20); no employer or ABN — check it.

**Case study:** basic pay rate, casual loading, evening and weekend penalty rates; on the hours × rate lines (rate too low, no weekend rate); a compliance notice is an official order to work out and pay back what's owed.

realityCheck: **Payslips are private.** Never require students to bring one. The sample payslip does the job.

**Rates change.** Pay rates change every July, and junior rates are changing: in March 2026 the Fair Work Commission decided to phase out junior rates for most 18–20 year olds under the retail, fast food and pharmacy awards. The change is provisionally due to start from December 2026, and under-18 rates are unchanged. Don't quote real rates; send students to the Pay Calculator.
**Some students are already being underpaid.** If a student thinks they are, the Fair Work Ombudsman (13 13 94) and the Young Workers Centre can help, and contact can be anonymous.
**Maths anxiety.** The maths is just multiplying and subtracting. Calculators are fine; the literacy is in knowing what to check.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's short and practical, and it follows straight on from Work Ready.
